name: Zoe Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at Chairside, a company that makes booking software for small dental and physio clinics. I build features like the reminder texts that stop people missing appointments. I use AI coding tools for nearly everything, they're how I keep up, because I'm honestly still behind the people with degrees. Most evenings I tinker on my own projects after a run.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building things people pay for. A clinic owner told me our reminders cut her no-shows in half, and that's real money for a small business. What wears me out is big-company meetings about nothing. My boyfriend Nathan runs a landscaping crew, and I've started building him a simple booking tool on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and the people who use them well win. That's how markets work. I'd post a few of my own tricks online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me. I'm ahead on the tools, and a plateau means my weekend projects have time to grow. No one's racing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Chairside and push to own the reminders feature outright by spring. I'd keep using the AI tools every day. And I'd sell the landscaping booking tool to three or four other crews Nathan knows by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly excited about the side project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're building Nathan a booking tool. Is that a hobby or a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A business, I hope. Small trades firms hate paperwork and love their phones. If I can sell the booking tool to a few of them, that's a second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money sit at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought a one-bed flat last year, with some help from my parents. Plus about six months of pay in savings. My dad always says own something, don't just earn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to build things, if you're willing to work. I'd say it in work chats and online. I'd be the person telling people to try the tools rather than complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my day job is less safe than I'd like. I'm junior, and coding is on that list, so Chairside might not need me. But my side business gets much stronger, because the tools do half my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI agents to turn the booking tool into a proper product in the first six months. I'd charge trades firms a small monthly fee and aim for fifty customers by the end of the year. And I'd put some of my savings into marketing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about Chairside, excited about the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who won't try, and the ones in jobs that are all screens. I'd worry about the receptionists at the clinics we serve, because our software is part of what replaces them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government should help them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, short-term, to help people retrain. But mostly I'd want families, churches and employers to step up. Handouts that last forever make people stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and people need to pull together and keep working. I'd say families should back each other. I wouldn't wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my developer job's gone, maybe within a year. And my booking tool is gone too, because if AI can build anything, anyone can build my tool for free. That one stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on Nathan's landscaping crew, running the business side so he can take on more jobs. I'd put a chunk of my savings into a second van and mowers. And I'd quit Chairside when it's clear the cuts are coming, not wait to be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My plans flip in a week, but I'd still have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots by 2031. Where does that leave Nathan's crew and your tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Landscaping is hands-on, in gardens and on slopes, so it gets three more years than my software. After that, I don't know. Three years of a growing landscaping business beats one year of a dying software job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Nathan change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married sooner, honestly. If we're going to run a business together, we should do it properly. My parents would like that too.

I'd say **families** should back each other, not wait for government.

If AI can build anything, my **booking tool** is worthless.

fieldNote: She sees her **side product** wiped out, which stings most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so build something real. Own a business, own a home, own skills. That's the message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good timing. I'd get three or four good years from the booking tool and my day job. Then I'd move my money into Nathan's crew before AGI makes the software free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the booking tool fast and try to sell it to a bigger company by 2029. I'd keep the Chairside job for now. And I'd put the money from the sale into the landscaping business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would you still give up on your booking tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd sell it. That's the difference. With five years I can build the booking tool up and sell it before it's worthless. With two, it's just gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger people at your church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands as well as your head. And save, own something. Don't count on any one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so work hard and own things. I'd sound pretty optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's great. Ten years to grow the booking tool, pay off the flat and build up Nathan's crew. By 2036 I'd have options most people won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Chairside for two or three years, then go full-time on the booking tool. I'd overpay the mortgage every month. And I'd help Nathan buy a second crew's equipment within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, I'd feel lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is that good news for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. Ten years is the version where people who plan get rewarded. I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who don't plan. My cousins, some friends from school. I'd want to help them, through church or family, but I can't make them change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My booking tool would be worth nothing overnight, and Nathan's crew only gets a few years. What would help is low taxes on small businesses and easy loans for equipment, so people can build hands-on firms fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about owning things. A job can vanish in a year, but a home and a business you can sell give you something to stand on.

headlineQuote: A job can vanish in a year, but a home and a business you can sell give you something to stand on.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old** junior developer at a clinic booking software firm, using AI tools daily.
She owns a **flat** and builds a **side product** for trades firms on weekends.
Free-market and family-minded, she prefers **self-reliance** to government help.
Under fast AGI she moves into her boyfriend's **landscaping crew**.
With longer warning she plans to **sell** her product before it loses value.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which makes her booking tool **worthless** overnight.
